points: Glucose and fructose occur naturally in fruit; fructose is also the main sugar in honey.
Galactose is not usually eaten free; it is released when lactose, the sugar in milk, is digested.
Glucose syrup, a refined sugar used in sweets and processed foods, is a source of glucose in the diet.
Sucrose, the table sugar, is extracted from sugar beet and sugar cane; it also occurs naturally in many fruit and vegetables.
Lactose is the sugar found in milk and milk products such as yoghurt and cheese.
Maltose is produced when starch is broken down during the germination of barley, the basis of malt.
Added sugars are found in biscuits, cakes, sweets, jam, fizzy drinks and breakfast cereals.
Potatoes, rice, pasta and bread are the main starch foods in the Irish diet.
Cereal grains such as wheat, oats, barley, maize and rice are rich sources of starch; flour is made from ground grain.
Pulses such as peas, beans and lentils, and root vegetables, contain starch as well as fibre.
Porridge oats and many breakfast cereals are starch-based.
Cellulose is found in the skins of fruit and vegetables, in leafy vegetables, in wholegrain cereals and in bran.
Pectin is found in the cell walls of fruit, especially apples and citrus fruit.
Wholemeal bread, brown rice and wholemeal pasta contain more fibre than white versions because the bran is retained in the grain.
Seeds such as sunflower, pumpkin, sesame and linseed are high in fibre, as are nuts and dried beans and lentils.
Settings: a collage or poster grouping foods by the type of carbohydrate they contain.

keyTerms.definition: The disaccharide made of glucose and fructose, extracted from sugar beet and sugar cane as table sugar.
The disaccharide made of glucose and galactose, found in milk and milk products.
The disaccharide made of two glucose units, produced when starch breaks down during the germination of barley.
A polysaccharide that is the main carbohydrate in cereals, potatoes, rice and pasta.
A non-starch polysaccharide found in the cell walls of fruit, especially apples and citrus fruit.
A plant polysaccharide, such as cellulose or pectin, that the human digestive system cannot break down and that forms dietary fibre.
The outer layer of a cereal grain, rich in cellulose and removed when grain is refined into white flour.

questions.prompt: Name one dietary source of a monosaccharide, one of a disaccharide and one of a polysaccharide.
questions.model: Monosaccharide: glucose from fruit, or fructose from honey. Disaccharide: sucrose from table sugar, or lactose from milk. Polysaccharide: starch from potatoes, or cellulose from the skins of vegetables.

questions.prompt: Give an account of the dietary sources of sugars, starch and non-starch polysaccharides, and explain how choosing particular sources can improve the nutritional quality of the diet.
questions.model: Sugars: table sugar, honey, fruit, milk (lactose), and added sugars in biscuits, cakes, sweets, jam, fizzy drinks and cereals. Starch: potatoes, rice, pasta, bread, flour, breakfast cereals, porridge oats, peas, beans and lentils. Non-starch polysaccharides: skins of fruit and vegetables, wholegrain cereals, bran, seeds, nuts, pulses, apples and citrus fruit (pectin). Improvement: wholegrain bread, brown rice and pasta replace white versions to add fibre; fresh fruit replaces sugary snacks and juice; whole fruit and vegetables eaten with the skins on; naturally sugar-containing foods such as milk and fruit supply vitamins and minerals alongside their sugar.
